fatal_flaws.claim: §1.3/D3: 'The GBP shortcut is a path, not a field — pasting a Google Maps link at step 1 skips steps 2–5… Biggest single conversion lever.' §2.5 pipeline: expand short link → 'Extract place_id / cid / (name + coords)' → 'Google Places Details with fields=id,displayName,formattedAddress,location,nationalPhoneNumber,regularOpeningHours,primaryType,rating,userRatingCount,reviews,photos'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The pipeline mixes two mutually exclusive APIs. `displayName`, `primaryType`, `regularOpeningHours`, `location` are Places API (New) field-mask names; Places API (New) `places.get` accepts ONLY a place resource name (`places/{place_id}`) — there is no `cid` parameter. The `?cid=` lookup is an undocumented endpoint on the LEGACY Place Details API, which Google moved to Legacy status and closed to new projects on 2025-03-01 (developers.google.com/maps/billing-and-pricing/march-2025). And this is the common case, not the edge case: `maps.app.goo.gl` / `g.page` short links expand to `/maps/place/<name>/data=!…!1s0x47c5…:0x<hex>` — an FID/CID pair, not a `ChIJ…` place_id. Google's own Place ID doc notes place IDs can expire; the CID→place_id direction is explicitly not derivable offline (a place ID contains two 64-bit values, the CID is only the second). So the highest-value path in the funnel resolves nothing for most pasted links, on a deprecated undocumented endpoint.
fatal_flaws.correction: Do not build D3 on link parsing. Use Places API (New) Text Search with the business name + the coords extracted from the URL as a location bias, present the top match as the 'Ben jij dit?' card, and store the returned `place_id`. That is one supported, documented call and it collapses D3 and the §1.3 P1 lookup into the same code path (and the same billed SKU). Budget for the fact that the pasted link then only supplies a location hint, not a guaranteed match — so the 34 s GBP-path target needs re-derivation.

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.5: 'Photos are referenced by Places photo URI at build time, not re-hosted in R2.' §5.5 act 5: 'blurhash placeholders morph to real photos.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Three separate breakages. (1) A Place Photo (New) `name` EXPIRES — Google's Place Photos doc states that when the name expires you must re-request Place Details/Text Search to get a new one. A static generated site with baked photo names goes to broken images. (2) Every `getMedia` request requires `key=API_KEY` in the URL. Hotlinking from a public tenant site puts your Maps API key in every visitor's HTML and bills you a Place Photos request per pageview, unreferrable and unrestricted-by-referrer if the key must also work server-side. (3) It also destroys the ~100 Lighthouse constraint for tenant sites: a third-party origin you cannot set cache-control on, cannot serve AVIF/srcset from, and cannot preload as an LCP candidate with any confidence.
fatal_flaws.correction: Do not put Google photos on generated sites at all. Use Places photos only inside the onboarding diff preview (short-lived, server-proxied, key stays in the Worker), and for the built site use uploaded media or Pexels/Unsplash stock — which the blueprint already specifies as the fallback and which permits hosting. §10 risk 1 correctly identifies the re-hosting ban but then designs a hotlink that is worse.

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.6: '"Schrijf het voor mij" → claude-opus-5, effort: "low", thinking: { type: "adaptive" }, stream: true, max_tokens: 400.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: On Claude Opus 5, thinking is ON by default (adaptive) and thinking tokens are output tokens counted against `max_tokens`. A 400-token ceiling with adaptive thinking will routinely be consumed entirely by the thinking block, returning `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` with an empty or truncated `text` block — the textarea streams nothing and the 'magic' silently fails. Separately, `output_config.format` structured output is not used here but the same trap applies to §2.2's classifier if its `max_tokens` is similarly small.
fatal_flaws.correction: For both micro-calls set `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` (accepted on Opus 5 at effort `high` or below) and raise `max_tokens` to ~1024. If you keep thinking on for quality, `max_tokens` must be several thousand. Also note the documented Opus 5 disabled-thinking pitfall: with thinking off, delete any 'don't reason' instruction and add an explicit 'do not include internal or system XML tags in your response' line, or `<thinking>` tags leak into the textarea.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5.5: act 3 `streaming` runs 12–45 s with 'skeleton blocks fill with real streamed copy, line by line'; §0 targets Submit→live P50 52 s, P90 88 s. §5.5 act 2 headline covers `api_call` + `thinking`.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Two compounding errors. (1) On Opus 5 the default is `thinking.display: "omitted"` — thinking blocks stream with EMPTY text. The spec never sets `display` anywhere. So between `message_start` and the first visible output token there is a long, literally silent gap whose length scales with `effort` (and the generation job defaults to `effort='high'` in 0005). Act 2's 3–12 s window is a guess with nothing driving it; act 3's copy does not begin at 12 s. (2) A multi-page site (home + services + about + contact + 2 blog posts + privacy + terms + JSON-LD) is realistically 20–40 K output tokens before thinking. Nothing in this document measures Opus 5 output throughput, and 52 s P50 is asserted, not derived. The entire 7-act theatre — the per-act windows, the τ=6 s asymptote, the 15 s stall line, the 45 s email-and-release — is calibrated against a number that was never measured.
fatal_flaws.correction: Set `thinking: {type: "adaptive", display: "summarized"}` so act 2 has real content to render, and drive act boundaries purely off SSE events with no time windows in the spec at all. Then measure: run 20 real generations, record wall-clock per phase, and rewrite §0's table from the p50/p90 you observe. Opus 5 supports fast mode (`speed: "fast"`, beta `fast-mode-2026-02-01`, up to ~2.5× output tok/s at $10/$50 per MTok) — that is the only real lever on this target and it is not mentioned once.

fatal_flaws.claim: §9: 'GET /api/v1/onboarding/bootstrap — locale, cf.country, industries JSON (ETag, cache-control: public, max-age=3600), existing draft'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: This response is declared publicly cacheable while its body contains the caller's existing draft — business name, full address, phone, email, description (§7.1 `Draft.values`). Cloudflare's edge cache, any corporate proxy, and any shared browser cache will serve one visitor's PII to the next. The body also varies by `locale` and `cf.country` with no `Vary` header specified, so even the industries payload is subject to cross-locale poisoning (a German visitor gets the Dutch taxonomy from cache).
fatal_flaws.correction: Split it. `GET /api/v1/onboarding/industries?locale=nl` → immutable, content-hashed URL, `public, max-age=31536000` (or `public, max-age=3600` + `Vary: Accept-Language`). `GET /api/v1/onboarding/draft` → `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, cookie-authenticated. Never return user data from an endpoint marked `public`.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7.5 layer 2: 'Idempotency-Key: <draft.idempotency_key> … The Worker INSERTs into generation_jobs relying on uq_jobs_idem; on SQLITE_CONSTRAINT it returns the existing job_id with 200.' §7.1: draft_id and idempotency_key are 'minted client-side'. §9: 'GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}/events'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: `uq_jobs_idem` in 0005 is a GLOBAL unique index, not scoped to org or draft. The key is chosen by the client and is a ULID — time-ordered and enumerable, not a secret. Submitting with another tenant's idempotency key hits the constraint and, by the spec's own rule, returns that tenant's `job_id` with a 200. §9 then lists `/api/v1/jobs/{id}/events` with no authorization requirement at all, so the attacker subscribes and streams a stranger's business name, address, phone, email and generated copy live. Same shape for `/start?job=job_…` replay in §5.5. This is a straightforward cross-tenant IDOR handed out by the double-submit design.
fatal_flaws.correction: Mint `idempotency_key` server-side with crypto randomness on first draft creation and store it in the signed `aib_draft` cookie. Scope the uniqueness to the draft: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_jobs_idem ON generation_jobs(org_id, idempotency_key)` — or at minimum verify the caller's cookie owns the row before returning the existing `job_id` (return 409 otherwise, never the id). Authorize `/api/v1/jobs/{id}/events` against the draft cookie or the session on every connect and every `Last-Event-ID` resume.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4.2: video max 200 MB, max duration 60 s, 'hero uses first 12 s'. §4.3: 'Videos are not transcoded client-side… we validate container/duration… and upload the original.' Hard constraint: generated tenant sites must hit ~100 Lighthouse.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Nothing in the allowed stack transcodes video. Workers cannot (128 MB isolate, no native codecs, CPU-bounded); R2 is object storage. So the user's original MOV/HEVC becomes the hero of a site that must score ~100. An HEVC-in-MOV file does not play in Chrome or Firefox at all. A 200 MB hero is an instant fail on every performance audit and on real 4G. The 'first 12 s' claim is also unimplementable without a transcode — you cannot byte-range a 12-second clip out of an arbitrary MP4 and have it be a valid standalone file. Cloudflare Stream would solve it but is a separate paid product with per-minute-stored and per-minute-delivered pricing, and it is not in the constraint list or the cost model.
fatal_flaws.correction: Either (a) drop user video in Phase 1 entirely — keep the poster frame you already extract at t=1.0 s and use stock video for the hero, which §4.1's skip card already sells beautifully; or (b) get Cloudflare Stream added to the constraint list and price it before Phase 1 ships. Also cut the 200 MB cap to something a European mobile uplink can actually finish inside the §4.6 20 s media-phase wait (~25 MB); at 5 Mbps up, 200 MB is 320 s and will never land in the generated site.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7.1: 'draft_id: "drf_" + ULID, minted client-side.' §7.6 rate limits: 'draft-description 8/min/draft · media/sign 40/hour/draft'. §6.5: 'Bot defence is Cloudflare Turnstile in invisible/managed mode on the submit call only.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Every expensive endpoint is keyed on an identifier the attacker mints for free, and the only bot check is on the one endpoint that isn't the cheapest to abuse. Mint N drafts → N × 8 Opus 5 streaming calls/min (`draft-description`), and N × 40 presigned R2 PUTs/hour at 200 MB each (`media/sign`) — an open file-upload relay on your bucket and an unmetered LLM bill on your Anthropic key. `classify-industry` has no rate limit listed at all. Even `submit` at '3/hour/IP' is weaker than it reads: the Workers rate-limiting binding is documented as enforcing 'a unique limit per Cloudflare location', i.e. per colo, not globally.
fatal_flaws.correction: Turnstile on first draft creation, not on submit — issue the signed `aib_draft` cookie only after a Turnstile pass, and key every per-draft limit on the server-signed draft_id. Add an IP-level ceiling behind each per-draft one. Add a per-draft lifetime cap for `draft-description` (say 10 total, not 8/min) and `media/sign` (13 = 12 photos + 1 video, not 40/hour). Delete the R2 objects under `drafts/{draft_id}/` in the same cron that purges expired drafts — §9 purges the row and leaks the bytes forever.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7.2: 'Rows land in onboarding_drafts and are hard-deleted by cron 30 days after last touch (GDPR data-minimisation).' Target audience: small local businesses in Europe.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The GDPR reasoning stops at retention and never reaches residency, which is the part that is irreversible. D1's `eu` jurisdiction can ONLY be set at database creation and cannot be added or updated afterwards (developers.cloudflare.com/d1/configuration/data-location). The repo's wrangler.toml has `database_id = "REPLACE_WITH_REAL_ID"` — the database is not created yet, so this is decidable today and undoable tomorrow. This spec puts full identifying business PII (name, address, phone, email, IP country, UA hash) into D1 for 30 days, pre-consent, for EU SMBs. Get it wrong and the fix at 10,000 tenants is a full export/reimport under a new database id with a rewrite of every binding. R2 (bucket-creation-time jurisdiction) and Durable Objects (`jurisdiction`/`locationHint` at stub creation) have the same property.
fatal_flaws.correction: Create the D1 database with `--location eu` jurisdiction, the R2 buckets with the `eu` jurisdiction, and pin DO stubs with `jurisdiction: 'eu'`, before writing a single row. If a jurisdiction is set, note that D1 read replicas are also confined to it, which is what you want here. Also: this design has an EU-market data-protection surface (Google Places, Anthropic, Pexels/Unsplash, Geoapify, Stripe) and mentions a DPA nowhere.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5.5: 'The job runs in a Durable Object per job_id, fanning SSE out to any number of connected clients.' §9 SSE contract: 'id = generation_job_events.id, so Last-Event-ID resumption is a single indexed range scan.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Two real costs. (1) WebSocket Hibernation is documented as supported ONLY when the DO acts as a WebSocket server (developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/websockets). SSE is a plain HTTP response, so the DO cannot hibernate and is billed for duration for the whole 45–180 s per connected client, per job, plus the 70–140 s idle window before eviction. (2) Worse architecturally: `generation_job_events.id` is `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`. You cannot know that id until the D1 INSERT returns — so making it the SSE `id` forces a D1 write round-trip to the single write primary into the critical path of every streamed frame. That is 20–100 ms of added latency per line of copy, which is precisely the act-3 'line by line' effect the design is buying.
fatal_flaws.correction: Use `seq` (DO-assigned, known before the write) as the SSE `id`. `uq_job_events_seq ON generation_job_events(job_id, seq)` already exists and gives you exactly the same single indexed range scan for `Last-Event-ID`. Then buffer events in DO memory, emit to the stream immediately, and flush to D1 in batches. Switch the fan-out to WebSockets with the Hibernation API to get the duration billing back. Also add SSE keepalive comments — nothing in the spec sends a heartbeat, and a stream that emits no bytes during a long silent thinking phase will be dropped by intermediaries.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7.6: 'Rate limits (via the existing rate_limit_buckets): lookup 30/min/IP · resolve-gbp 10/min/IP · draft-description 8/min/draft · media/sign 40/hour/draft · submit 3/hour/IP + 1/draft.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: This directly contradicts the repo it is written against. wrangler.toml already declares two rate-limit bindings and carries the comment: 'Per-request rate limiting belongs HERE, never in D1.' Routing per-request limiting through the D1 `rate_limit_buckets` table (0007) puts a read-modify-write to the single D1 write primary on the hot path of the keystroke-triggered lookup and the 1200 ms autosave — for EU users that primary round-trip is added to every debounce settle. Two people have made opposite architectural decisions and neither has noticed. (Also: the declared bindings use the legacy `[[unsafe.bindings]]` form; the GA form is `[[ratelimits]]`.)
fatal_flaws.correction: Resolve it explicitly in the doc: use the Workers rate-limit binding for per-request limits (and state, as the docs do, that it is per-colo and approximate, so set per-colo budgets accordingly and stop claiming `Retry-After` from it — the binding returns only `{success}`). Keep `rate_limit_buckets` for slow, cross-colo, money-spending counters only — `submit` and lifetime per-draft LLM caps — where a D1 write per event is affordable and global accuracy actually matters.

fatal_flaws.claim: §2.1 Shortcuts (b): 'Live slug: lowercase → NFKD → strip diacritics → [^a-z0-9]+→- → collapse -- → trim - → 63 char cap.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: For any business name in a non-Latin script the pipeline yields the empty string. NFKD does not transliterate Greek, Cyrillic, or Han — it only decomposes combining marks — so 'Ελληνικό Καφέ' or 'Кафе Мечта' becomes ''. `sites.slug` in 0003 is `CHECK (length(slug) BETWEEN 3 AND 63 AND slug GLOB '[a-z0-9]*')`. The failure therefore surfaces as a CONSTRAINT error inside the submit `batch()` — after the user has spent the full 82 s, at the exact moment §0 calls the peak-end moment. Greece, Cyprus and Bulgaria are in the stated target market. Separately, appending '-<city>' after the 63-char cap can push the result back over 63.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add a transliteration step (a small ICU-style map or `@sindresorhus/transliterate`) before the character filter, and a terminal fallback: if the slug is still shorter than 3 chars, use `<industry_key>-<city>` or a short random suffix. Enforce the 63-char cap AFTER collision suffixing, not before. Validate the final slug server-side at `/slug-check` time so the failure surfaces at step 1, never at submit.

fatal_flaws.claim: §7.6: 'navigator.connection.saveData or effectiveType ∈ {slow-2g,2g} → skip the static map thumbnail, skip stock-photo previews, drop image compression target to 1200 px, and reduce upload concurrency to 1.' §8.8: the video src is 'never [attached] when saveData or effectiveType ∈ {slow-2g,2g,3g}'.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The Network Information API (`navigator.connection`, `effectiveType`, `saveData`) is not implemented in Safari or Firefox. On iOS — the dominant mobile browser for this audience — `navigator.connection` is `undefined`, so every one of these guards silently evaluates to 'fast connection'. Every iPhone on a bad 3G connection downloads the 2.8 MB hero video, uploads at concurrency 3, and gets the full-size compression target. Two of this document's headline claims (the Lighthouse story in §8.8 and the entire slow-network section in §7.6) rest on an API that is absent on roughly half the target devices, and the spec asserts a hard 2.8 MB cap as if the guard were reliable.
fatal_flaws.correction: Feature-detect and treat absence as 'unknown', not 'fast'. Use measurable proxies that work everywhere: time the poster fetch and skip the video if it exceeded a threshold; use `prefers-reduced-data` where available; make the video opt-in on any viewport under 640 px rather than opt-out. Keep `saveData` as a bonus signal, never as the gate.

fatal_flaws.claim: §0/D4: 'Email is the last field of the last step, framed as delivery, not signup.' §9 submit: 'user+org+site+job in one batch()'. §5.5 act 8: site live at <slug>.mijnsaas.com.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The site is published to a public subdomain before the email is ever verified. Combined with §2.5, that public page can carry a real third party's business name, verified address, phone number, opening hours and Google reviews, pulled from their GBP listing by someone who is not them. That is an impersonation surface, a defamation surface, and — because you are publishing another data subject's identifying business data without any lawful basis — a straightforward GDPR problem in the exact market you are targeting. Squatting a real business's email also permanently blocks the real owner: `uq_users_email` is unique on `email_normalized`, and §7.5 layer 4 caps one `initial_site` job per org, so the genuine owner hits the 409 path.
fatal_flaws.correction: Publish to a `noindex` preview URL until the email is verified, and only promote to the indexable `<slug>.mijnsaas.com` after a click-through. Serve `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` on unverified sites. Add an abuse-report route on every generated site and a claim flow for the real owner. This is a one-line HTTP header now and a legal problem later.

fatal_flaws.claim: §3.1's 104-row taxonomy and §9 item 3: 'Seed all 14 groups + the 104 rows of §3.1, with design_preset carrying "dna" and the §3.2 expansion.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: 0009 is already applied and wrangler.toml states the rule: 'Forward-only: never edit an applied migration.' Several of §3.1's rows contradict rows that already exist. `dj` is seeded as `schema_org_type='MusicGroup'`; §3.1 row 72 says `LocalBusiness` + a wikidata `additionalType`. `physiotherapist` is seeded as `'Physician'`; §3.1 row 19 says `Physiotherapy`. `industries.key` is the PRIMARY KEY, so a plain INSERT of the 104 rows fails on conflict for every already-seeded key. §9 describes this as additive seeding and says nothing about the collision or the type changes.
fatal_flaws.correction: 0010 needs explicit `INSERT … ON CONFLICT(key) DO UPDATE SET schema_org_type=excluded.schema_org_type, design_preset=excluded.design_preset, …` for the overlapping keys, and the doc should say which existing rows it is changing and why. Also fix `tour_operator` — `TouristInformationCenter` is a place where tourists get information, not a tour operator; use `TravelAgency` or `LocalBusiness` + additionalType. And the `tailor` row is marked † ('no adequate subtype') while being assigned the real type `ClothingStore`, which contradicts your own footnote definition.

fatal_flaws.claim: §6.2: '2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum): the sticky footer with the primary button is position: sticky; bottom: 0 — the scroll container therefore carries scroll-padding-bottom … Also padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom).'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` is the home-indicator/notch inset. It has nothing to do with the software keyboard. On iOS Safari the layout viewport does not shrink when the keyboard opens, so a `position: sticky; bottom: 0` footer sits underneath the keyboard the moment any field is focused — which is exactly the 2.4.11 failure this paragraph claims to have solved, on the primary conversion button, on the majority platform. `scroll-padding-bottom` does not help because the footer is not the thing being scrolled to. Chrome Android needs `interactive-widget=resizes-content` in the viewport meta, which is not specified either.
fatal_flaws.correction: Drive the footer offset from `window.visualViewport` (`resize` + `scroll` listeners, offset = `layoutViewportHeight - visualViewport.height - visualViewport.offsetTop`), or place the primary button in normal flow below the field on touch instead of sticky. Add `interactive-widget=resizes-content` to the viewport meta. Then actually test steps 5 and 6 on a real iPhone before claiming 2.4.11.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5.5 failure handling: only 'Dit duurt iets langer dan normaal' at 15 s of silence and email-and-release at 45 s. §9 lists no refusal path.
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Claude Opus 5 can decline a request with HTTP 200, `stop_reason: "refusal"`, and a `stop_details.category` — not an exception, not a 4xx. The input here is free text a stranger typed about their business, so this will happen. The spec's error handling assumes failures look like timeouts or 5xx. A refusal at t=8 s produces a 200 with no usable content and the theatre keeps animating toward a reveal that will never come. `generation_jobs.stop_reason` exists in 0005 but no phase, no act, and no copy handles it. Relatedly, current Anthropic guidance is to send the server-side `fallbacks` parameter on Opus 5 requests by default (beta `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01`, `fallbacks: "default"`); it appears nowhere.
fatal_flaws.correction: Check `stop_reason` before touching `content` on every call. Add a `phase='error'` branch (the enum already has it) with honest copy and a 'try a different description' route back into step 6 with the draft intact. Enable server-side fallbacks on the generation call so a refusal routes to another model instead of dead-ending the funnel.

fatal_flaws.why_wrong: These were asserted, not measured, despite the word 'verified'. Computing WCAG 2.x relative luminance: #101828 on white is 17.7:1 (not 16.1); #667085 on white is 4.97:1 (not 5.3); #B42318 on white is 6.6:1 (not 6.4). #475467 at 7.69:1 and #1F44DB at 7.22:1 are correct. Every value still passes its threshold, so nothing is broken — but #667085 at 4.97:1 has far less headroom than 5.3 implies, and the same paragraph asserts 'smallest text is 12 px' while §8.2 defines `--text-2xs: 11px`.
fatal_flaws.correction: Re-run the whole ramp through a checker and paste real numbers, or drop the word 'verified'. Fix the 11 px vs 12 px contradiction. A reviewer who spot-checks one number and finds it wrong stops trusting the other forty.

fatal_flaws.claim: §5.5: 'Seven acts, mapped 1:1 onto the generation_job_events.phase enum that already exists.' §10 risk 3 restates this as an invariant: 'The 7-act theatre in §5.5 is mapped onto exactly those 12 values on purpose.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The table immediately below contradicts it. Act 2 is `api_call` + `thinking` (two phases), act 4 is `parsing` + `pages_written` (two phases), and the table has nine rows (acts 0–8), not seven. So the mapping is many-to-one, which means the client cannot derive the act from the phase alone — it needs a lookup table that the spec never provides, and an event arriving in `thinking` after the UI has moved past `api_call` has undefined behaviour.
fatal_flaws.correction: Publish the explicit `phase → act` map as data, and define what the client does on an out-of-order or repeated phase (the safe rule: acts advance monotonically; a lower-act phase updates the detail line without moving the rail backwards). Then say 'many-to-one' instead of '1:1' in §10.

fatal_flaws.claim: §6.1: 'role="document" on the inner panel keeps JAWS/NVDA in browse mode for the helper prose.' §6.4: 'The polite region is cleared to \'\' for one frame before each new message.' §6.2: initial focus 'set after the 320 ms entrance completes.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Three small a11y errors in an otherwise strong section. (1) NVDA/JAWS switch to focus/forms mode based on the focused control, not on the dialog — `role="document"` was guidance for `role="application"` containers and is cargo cult inside a `<dialog>`; some ATs announce the extra node. (2) One animation frame (~16 ms) is generally too short for a screen reader to observe the mutation and re-announce; the working technique needs a real tick or alternating regions. (3) `showModal()` already moves focus (to `[autofocus]` or the first focusable). Moving it again 320 ms later produces a double focus event and a yanked, half-read announcement — the opposite of the stated intent.
fatal_flaws.correction: Drop `role="document"`. Clear the live region and set the new text on separate ticks ~100 ms apart, or alternate between two polite regions. Put `autofocus` on the intended target so `showModal()` lands focus once, correctly, at t=0, and drop the 320 ms deferral.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4.1 accept list: 'image/jpeg,image/png,image/webp,image/heic,image/heif,video/mp4,video/quicktime'. §4.2 Accepted: 'JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, HEIC/HEIF'. §4.6 wrong-type copy: 'Gebruik JPG, PNG, WebP of MP4.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Three different lists in three adjacent sections. AVIF is accepted in the limits table but missing from the `accept` attribute (so the file picker filters it out on desktop). MOV and HEIC are accepted by the input but the error message tells the user they cannot be used. Whichever list the implementer copies, one of the other two becomes a bug or a lie to the user.
fatal_flaws.correction: Define the accepted set once as a constant, generate the `accept` attribute and the error copy from it, and make the server-side magic-byte sniff in §4.4 validate against the same constant.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4.3: 'Runs in a dedicated Web Worker so the main thread never drops a frame… HEIC on non-Safari falls back to a lazily-imported heic2any chunk.' §10 risk 4: 'Roughly a third of iPhone uploads in the EU are HEIC.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The catch is genuinely good — Chrome and Firefox really cannot decode HEIC — but two details are wrong. `heic2any` bundles libheif as WASM at roughly 1.4 MB and is not worker-safe out of the box (it reaches for DOM APIs), so it lands on the main thread and blows the 'never drops a frame' guarantee precisely on the slowest devices. And the premise is overstated for this input path: iOS Safari transcodes HEIC to JPEG by default when a photo is chosen through `<input type="file">`; HEIC mainly arrives via macOS drag-and-drop and desktop Finder, which is a much smaller share than 'a third of iPhone uploads'.
fatal_flaws.correction: Prefer `libheif-js` (or a worker-wrapped build) so the decode really is off-thread, and show an explicit 'converting…' tile state since it will take seconds on a mid-range phone. Restate risk 4 as 'HEIC arrives mainly from desktop drag-and-drop' — it is still worth handling, but sizing it wrongly will get the fallback cut in a scope review.

fatal_flaws.claim: §8.8: '<video autoplay muted loop playsinline preload="none" poster="hero-1600.avif">, poster preloaded with fetchpriority="high" — the poster is the LCP element' plus 'a 9:16 crop for (max-width: 640px) via <source media> so phones never download the wide file.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: The LCP reasoning is correct — Chrome uses the poster image load time or the first-frame presentation time, whichever is earlier, so a preloaded poster with a late-attached src does win. But `poster` is a single attribute on `<video>`; `<source media>` art-directs the video only. So the 9:16 mobile treatment ships a landscape 1600 px AVIF poster to a portrait phone, where `object-fit: cover` throws away most of the pixels you just paid LCP for — on the mobile Lighthouse run that is the one that matters. Separately, four font preloads (Inter Tight + Inter, latin + latin-ext) compete with that `fetchpriority="high"` poster for the initial bandwidth on a throttled run.
fatal_flaws.correction: Set the poster from a `<picture>`/CSS background layered under the video, or swap `video.poster` from a tiny inline script keyed to a media query, so the portrait crop gets a portrait poster. Preload one weight of one family (Inter) and let Inter Tight arrive with `font-display: swap` — you already tune `size-adjust`, so the CLS cost is near zero and the LCP win is real.

fatal_flaws.claim: §4.4: 'POST /api/v1/onboarding/media/sign → Worker returns an R2 presigned PUT (S3 API), 15-minute expiry… Uploads go browser → R2 directly via XMLHttpRequest.'
fatal_flaws.why_wrong: Correct on the mechanics — R2 supports presigned PUT (presigned POST is not supported, and you are not using it), and R2's S3 PutObject supports `x-amz-checksum-sha256` — but the bucket-side prerequisite is missing. Cloudflare's docs are explicit that browser requests to a presigned URL on a different origin are still subject to CORS, and that without a bucket CORS policy browser uploads fail even though the presigned URL itself is valid. `AllowedHeaders` must also enumerate every header you bind into the signature (`content-length`, `x-amz-checksum-sha256`) or the preflight rejects them.
fatal_flaws.correction: Add the R2 bucket CORS policy to the Phase 1 checklist: `AllowedOrigins` = your marketing origin, `AllowedMethods` = PUT, `AllowedHeaders` = content-type, content-length, x-amz-checksum-sha256, `ExposeHeaders` = etag (needed to assemble multipart). Note it in §9 alongside the endpoints — it is the kind of thing that only fails in staging.

missing: A video transcode path. §4.3 explicitly declines to transcode and no server-side path exists in the allowed stack — this is the load-bearing gap between §4 and the ~100 Lighthouse constraint. Either Cloudflare Stream gets added to the constraints with its per-minute-stored and per-minute-delivered pricing modelled, or user video is cut from Phase 1.

Unit economics for the free generation. Claude Opus 5 is $5/MTok input and $25/MTok output, and thinking tokens bill as output. A full site at 20–40K output tokens plus adaptive thinking at effort='high' (the default in 0005) is roughly $0.75–$1.50 per generation. D5 gives that away with no card, and §0 targets ≥46% of modal-opens reaching a completed generation. Nowhere does the document state cost per free generation, expected free→paid conversion, or a monthly AI budget ceiling. Against €9,99/mo billed annually this is the number the whole funnel design should have been optimised around.

Google Places cost modelling. Text Search is billed per request (not per session like Autocomplete), Pro tier is ~$32/1000, and the universal $200/month credit was replaced on 2025-03-01 by per-SKU free tiers (10k Essentials / 5k Pro / 1k Enterprise per month). §1.3 fires a Text Search on every 400 ms debounce settle from 3 characters — several billed calls per user who merely starts step 1, including every bouncer. No budget, no per-session dedupe, no cheaper-SKU fallback is specified.

Onboarding localisation beyond NL/EN. Every label, helper, error and act headline is written twice; `Draft.locale` allows six locales and the product promises /en/ /nl/ /de/ /fr/ /es/ /pt/. Four locales of UI copy are missing with no note on who writes them or when.

The real content cost of §9 item 4: 104 leaves × 6 locales = 624 `industry_translations` rows, each needing a localised label plus 'minimum 6 aliases'. That is roughly 3,700 hand-authored alias strings, called 'this column IS the search quality' and then filed as a one-line migration note. It is the largest single unowned work item in Phase 1.

Authorization model for `/api/v1/jobs/{id}/events` and for `/start?job=job_…` replay. §9 lists the endpoint; nothing states who may subscribe, or how `Last-Event-ID` resume is authorized on reconnect.
SSE keepalive. Nothing sends heartbeat comments during the long silent thinking phase, so intermediaries will drop streams that the design assumes stay open for 45–180 s.

Lawful basis for the pre-consent identifiers. `aib_draft` is a 30-day cookie set at step-1 keystroke 3, and `localStorage` holds business name, address, phone and email indefinitely with no stated clear-on-submit. §7.2 argues retention but never argues the ePrivacy/consent basis, and this product ships a cookie banner for its tenants while not analysing its own.
Deletion of R2 objects on draft expiry. §9 purges the `onboarding_drafts` row after 30 days; `drafts/{draft_id}/*` is never deleted, so every abandoned upload is stored forever.

Google attribution in the onboarding diff preview. §2.5 correctly requires visible attribution on the generated site's reviews but the 'We vonden 11 gegevens' consent screen — which displays Places name, address, hours, rating and photos — carries none.

What a partial generation looks like. Acts 3–7 assume forward progress; there is no defined state for 'four pages written, media_fetch failed', no partial-publish rule, and no copy for it — even though `site_versions.status` already models 'building'.
Cloudflare Stream / Images, Turnstile, Geoapify and Pexels/Unsplash all appear as dependencies but none appear in wrangler.toml or in any cost or rate-limit budget.
verdict: The UX craft here is genuinely strong and I do not want to damn it by summary: the wizard-vs-chat argument is right, the chip-first opening-hours design (presets before the grid, `<select>` over `<input type=\"time\">`, 15-minute steps, 24h) is the correct call and better than what Wix ships, the WCAG 2.2 work is real rather than decorative (2.5.7 keyboard reordering, 3.3.7 redundant entry, the 3.3.8/Turnstile reasoning, `showModal()` instead of a hand-rolled trap with no manual `aria-modal`), stripping GPS EXIF is a GDPR catch most teams miss, the `libphonenumber-js/max` lazy-load rationale is technically exact, `draft_media` as a staging table instead of relaxing `media_assets.site_id` is the right instinct, `PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys` in a `batch()` is genuinely supported by D1, and the poster-as-LCP claim survives verification against Chrome's actual rule. That is a rare hit rate. But the spec is not sound enough to build on yet, because its three highest-leverage claims are each false at a level that changes the product. D3 — 'the biggest single conversion lever' — is built on a `cid` lookup that exists only on Google's legacy, closed-to-new-projects Place Details API while using Places API (New) field names, so it resolves nothing for the short links users actually paste. The 45–90 s generation theatre, which every number in §0 and every act in §5.5 depends on, was never measured and is contradicted by two documented Opus 5 behaviours the spec never accounts for: thinking is on by default and `thinking.display` defaults to `\"omitted\"`, so act 3 does not begin when the timeline says it does. And §4's 200 MB untranscoded hero video cannot coexist with the ~100 Lighthouse constraint in a stack with no transcoder. Underneath those sit three security holes that are cheap to close now and expensive later: a `public, max-age=3600` bootstrap endpoint that returns the caller's draft PII, a client-minted global idempotency key that hands out other tenants' `job_id`s to an unauthenticated event stream, and client-minted `draft_id`s gating the R2 signer and the Opus 5 description drafter with Turnstile placed on the one endpoint that is not the cheapest to abuse. The single most urgent item is not in the UX at all: D1's `eu` jurisdiction can only be set at database creation and never changed, `database_id` is still `REPLACE_WITH_REAL_ID`, and this spec puts EU business PII in D1 for 30 days pre-consent — that decision has hours left to be free and is a full migration at 10,000 tenants. Fix the six fatals, set the jurisdictions, then measure one real generation end-to-end and rewrite §0's table from what you observe rather than from what the choreography needs to be true.
